utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce Catherine Connelly, from Australia, who is one of our legal interns who will be joining us this session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we continue with Mr. Spasojevic's -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: His evidence, there are three oral rulings the Chamber wishes to give at the moment. First matter is related to the Prosecution's request for deferral of cross-examination of subpoenaed viva voce witnesses. On the 19th of March, 2013, the Prosecution requested that cross-examination of subpoenaed witnesses be, as a matter of principle, postponed for two weeks until after examination-in-chief of the said witnesses. In support, the Prosecution claims that it is not aware whether these witnesses will ultimately testify and that it has not been notified of the facts upon which these witnesses will testify. The accused's legal advisor supported the Prosecution's request and submitted that the Prosecution should be given some period of time to prepare after examination-in-chief of subpoenaed viva voce witnesses. The Chamber does not consider that the Prosecution's request is warranted. Subpoenaed witnesses will necessarily testify viva voce and, as such, there's obviously no need for Rule 92 ter material to be disclosed ahead of testimony. In the case of witnesses who are persons previously convicted by the Tribunal, such as Radislav Krstic and Zdravko Tolimir, the Prosecution, as does the Defence, has access to a plethora of material gathered over a number of years and to the entire record of their respective trials. Moreover, for all subpoenaed witnesses, the Prosecution will be able to refer to the relevant motions in which the accused sets out the contours of what he expects the said witness to testify about. The Chamber is therefore of the view that in cases of subpoenaed witnesses who are testifying viva voce, the Prosecution should be able to start its cross-examination at the end of examination-in-chief by the accused. Of course, there may be instances where good cause having been shown by the Prosecution, a short delay before cross-examination is warranted. Next matter is related to counsel for Milan Martic. The Chamber is seized of detained witness Milan Martic's complaint against the decision of the Registry denying the request to assign Defence counsel filed on the 19th of March, 2013. In Martic's submission, he informs the Chamber that he has requested that his attorney, Predrag Milovancevic, act as counsel, both prior to and during his testimony as part of the accused's Defence case. Martic notes that the Registry has not granted this request, and that he and the Registry have been unable to reach agreement regarding alternative arrangements with other proposed counsel. On the 20th of March, 2013, the Prosecution orally informed the Chamber that it did not take a position on this matter but noted that, pursuant to, inter alia, Rule 44(B) of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Martic's submission should be reviewed by the President. On 20th of March, 2013, the accused filed the submission in support of Milan Martic's appeal on assignment of counsel in support of Martic's submission and furthermore requested that the Chamber vacate its order, issued orally on the 13th of March, 2013, that Martic testify during the week of 25th of March, 2013, because no proofing has yet taken place. During a hearing on the 21st of March, the accused's legal advisor argued that the Trial Chamber is competent to rule on the submission. The Chamber considers that matters related to the assignment of counsel, pursuant to Rule 45 of the Rules, fall under the authority of the President of the Tribunal and finds that there are no circumstances in this case that warrant its involvement in the interests of justice. The Chamber therefore dismisses Martic's complaint as not properly filed before the Chamber. Furthermore, given the urgency of the matter and the interest of judicial economy, the Chamber requests that the relevant filings and transcripts of oral submissions be immediately transmitted to the President. Finally, given that proofing has not yet commenced, the Chamber will vacate its oral ruling of 13th of March, 2013, that Martic be called to testify during the week of 25th -- 25th of March, 2013. Once the President has made his determination, the Chamber will return to the issue of appropriate date for Martic's testimony. Finally, the Chamber shall now issue an oral ruling in relation to the accused's motion for disclosure of records pertaining to Milan Babic, filed publicly on the 18th of March, 2013, in which the accused requests, pursuant to Rule 54 of the Tribunal's Rules of Procedure and Evidence, as well as Rule 34 of the Rules of Detention, that the Chamber order the Registry to disclose to him all psychological evaluations of Milan Babic. He argues that this is necessary as the information sought goes to the credibility of Babic whose evidence from previous cases was admitted in this case pursuant to Rule 92 quater. The accused claims that he was only recently informed by the upcoming witness, Milan Martic, that Babic may have been diagnosed with a personality disorder while at the detention unit. He also notes that these psychological evaluation were made available to Judge Parker who conducted an inquiry into Babic's suicide in 2006, as referred to in the report prepared by Judge Parker following this inquiry. The Prosecution responded to the accused's motion on the 20th of March, 2013, arguing that it should be denied on the basis that the medical information sought is highly confidential and that the accused has failed to show that confidential medical information confirming the existence of a personality disorder even exists. In the alternative, the Prosecution argues that the Chamber should examine the medical information in-camera to determine whether it is relevant to any of the issues in this case, before ordering its disclosure. The Registry also responded to the motion on the 20th of March, 2013, arguing that it should be denied on the basis that the second-hand unconfirmed rumour by Martic does not approach the threshold required for the Trial Chamber to overturn the principle of medical confidentiality enshrined in Rules 11 and 34(C) of the Rules of Detention. Having considered the arguments made by the parties, the Chamber finds that it is in the interests of justice and the good administration of this trial that the psychological evaluation of Babic be first disclosed to the Chamber for an in-camera inspection so that it can determine whether they contain any information that may be relevant to the accused's case. In coming to this conclusion, the Chamber considered the fact that Babic's evidence was admitted under Rule 92 quater and that, therefore, the accused was devoid of an opportunity to cross-examine him. The Chamber was also not persuaded by the main crux of the Prosecution's and the Registry's responses to the effect that, by relying on Martic, the accused has made no genuine effort to demonstrate that Babic's medical information would be relevant and necessary to his case. Given the highly confidential nature of the medical documentation sought, it is not clear to the Chamber how the accused could have obtained more information or done more to support this motion. Accordingly, the Chamber orders the Registrar, pursuant to Rule 54 of the Rules, to provide the Chamber with the copies of any reports or information on the psychological state of Milan Babic while at the detention unit. The Chamber shall then inspect these psychological evaluations in-camera before deciding whether they should be disclosed to the accused. Unless there are any other matters -- Yes, we received the go from Judge Lattanzi. French translation has been just completed. Yes Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's nice to see the shoe on the other foot. I just wanted to make one note, Mr. President. The Court has been dealing with, during the course of this week, various problems arising from the e-court upgrade. I wanted to note that those problems persist after court. And indeed what seems to be happening and what was reflected over the course of the last two nights is that e-court is not available after court and then is fixed immediately before court. Now, that -- so the process appears to be less troublesome than it has been in court, but in effect is inaccessible to the parties at critical periods. We're making efforts to bring it to the attention of the relevant arms of the Tribunal so it can be addressed, but I simply wanted to note that because it has a tremendous impact on the parties' ability to prepare. And it hasn't delayed things yet, but with the weekend coming up, I'm concerned about what kind of impact it may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It is duly noted, Mr. Tieger. Shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: While we have some time and we're bringing in the witness, I would -- with respect to those -- those oral rulings that you made today, some of them are quite important for the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. I think the issue of the jurisdiction of Mr. Martic's complaint as well as the inspection of the witness's psychological records are issues of first impression at the Tribunal, and when you make an oral ruling, it doesn't really lend itself to being available to others in the jurisprudence. And I was wondering whether the Chamber might consider making some -- putting some cover page and making a written record of your oral decisions so that it is entered into the database of the Tribunal and can be researched and located by people who are studying these things. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That seems to be the sort of idea that I'm hearing for the first time. The Chamber will give it a think. Good morning, Mr. Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And good morning, Mr. Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 24806, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Spasojevic, when we concluded yesterday, we were discussing the multiple murder of members of the Sarajlic and other families, and today I'd like to turn to another criminal event involving a murder and rape against Muslim civilians in Bijeljina and this was a crime that the police in Bijeljina actually did investigate at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 38 in both languages of this document, which is a Humanitarian Law Centre report on Serbian war crimes trials in 2012.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of the page this report refers to the 2012 conviction of Dragan Jovic, Zoran Djurdjevic and Alen Ristic by the higher court in Belgrade. Now you testified in that trial in 2011 in relation to an investigation you conducted in 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we he could go to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At the top of the page, under "Course of Proceedings," the indictment against the accused is summarised. And it explains that on -- the allegations were that on the 14th of June, 1992, in Bijeljina, the three accused, together with two others, entered the house of Ramo Avdic, seeking weapons. After a hand-over of weapons, they took money and jewellery, then raped Mr. Ramo's daughter and daughter-in-law, in the presence of Mr. Avdic's wife and son. Then they killed Mr. Avdic by placing a gun into his mouth and pulling the trigger. They then took the two women who they had already raped, paraded them naked through the town, stole a car from a nearby house, drove the two women towards the village of Ljeljenca, stopped the car, took the two women out of the car, raped and sexually abused them again, and left them at the side of the road? Now is that information the same or similar to the information you gathered about this crime at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it is completely truthful. I would just add something, if I may, and that was the check-point that you asked me about yesterday. It had a very important role, because you suggested yesterday the volunteers had set up the check-points. It was the police employees who set up the check-points. We had five of these, and the aim was to prevent such acts and also looting and thefts and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: What check-point are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the check-point in the direction of Brcko. That was where these persons were stopped and arrested. And we had another four, if I'm not mistaken, in the direction of Raca, Zvornik and Ugljevik, so I think there were four or five check-points but they were all police check-points.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go down to not the immediately following paragraph but the one after that, the summary says: "Testifying in their own defence, the accused said they went to Bosnia as volunteers, under the auspices of the Serb Radical Party, and when they arrived Bosnia, the VRS supplied them with uniforms and weapons." Now is that consistent with information you gathered at the time, about the accused?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go to the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And towards the bottom of the first full paragraph, it refers to your involvement. It says -- in the trial. It says: "Also questioned were witnesses Dusan Spasojevic, a police inspector, and Milorad Lovre, a crime scene technician, both working at the Bijeljina SUP at the time. Immediately after the injured parties reported the crime, the two men performed an investigation and obtained medical documentation for the injured parties, Nizama and Hajreta." And again, is this an accurate description of what you told the court in 2011 and what you did at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And in the next paragraph about four lines down, the summary says: "On the basis of their own testimonies," and they're talking about the testimony of accused, "and the testimonies of witnesses Dusan Spasojevic," you, "and Ramo Fazic, the court established that the injured parties were civilians and that the victim Ramo Avdic was no Muslim extremist but a reservist at the Bijeljina SUP, a wealthy and respected man actively involved in efforts towards a peaceful settlement of conflicts between Serbs and Muslims in Bijeljina." Now, is that -- can you confirm these facts and is that consistent with what you told the court in 2011?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to the next page in both languages. And this is towards the bottom of the first full paragraph in English and near the bottom of the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It says: "The fact that the accused took money and valuables while in the house was established both on the basis of the injured parties' testimonies and the testimony of witness Dusan Spasojevic, who said that during the arrest, the police found money and gold jewellery on the accused and returned it to the injured parties." And there's a footnote after the word "arrest" and at the bottom of the page it says: "The defendants were arrested by the Bijeljina police department following the incident and handed over to the military police who released them a couple of days, after which the defendants went to an area in the Zvornik municipality and joined the paramilitary formation Simo's Chetniks." And again, is that consistent with information you gathered at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the persons were uniformed, we could keep them detained for three days in detention on remand, and they were then handed over to the military police who expelled them in the territory of Serbia but they could have arrived in Zvornik by some other way.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you confirm that the military authorities didn't process this crime but they, as you put it, expelled the accused?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the statements were taken from them and forwarded to a military court, and that 15 or 20 days later, as far as I can remember, they were expelled to the territory of Serbia because there were no conditions to initiate proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Can you explain what you mean by "no conditions to initiate proceedings"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proceedings were actually initiated in terms of the documents that were collected, and everything else that it was possible to collect, it was collected. But I think that the military court was just being established and they had no premises and so on, so I believe that that was how things went and that those were the reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just intervene about the transcript because the witness said conditions for conducting proceedings rather than initiating proceedings and these were problems with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Whether it is translation issue, we'll leave it. But this document says "a couple of days later." But you said "15 or 20 days later." Do you have any basis that this document we are seeing is not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not claim that it is not correct, but Bijeljina is a small town, and I went to a cafe with the policeman that I handed them over to, and he told me that they were expelled to Serbia. This is it how I got this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But how long after were they expelled? After being handed over to the military police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps they were in the police prison on remand three days until statements were taken from them and the other documents prepared. Because they were wearing uniforms, after three days they were handed over to the military police, and I could even claim that they were up to 30 days held in the military police remand prison but I cannot claim that with full certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Spasojevic, if the military court wasn't sufficiently prepared to deal with this crime, why weren't they then just handed back to the civilian authorities to deal with? Why instead were the perpetrators of this terrible crime allowed to go free?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to tender page -- the cover page of this document and pages 38 to 42, which discuss this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And one last question on this document, Mr. Spasojevic. This report indicates that the Belgrade Higher Court did indeed convict these three defendants of this crime in June 2012. Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I went to testify there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you are aware that they were ultimately convicted; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But you have no reason to doubt the assertion in this report that the Belgrade Higher Court entered a conviction; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any suspicions regarding the court anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And after these perpetrators were released or expelled, as you put it, by the military police, there was nothing done about this crime for years, and it was only in 2009 that the Bijeljina prosecutor's office opened an investigation into this case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to 65 ter 24795, please. This is the 2009 order from the Bijeljina prosecutor's office to the SJB Bijeljina to open an investigation into this case. And if we go to page 3 of the English, and page 3 of the B/C/S, at the bottom of the English, the very top of the B/C/S, the document says: "The order can be justified by the following circumstances and evidence." And if we go to the next page in the English there is a list of all the investigative steps that were taken. And we can see a number of steps taken in the days immediately after this crime by the Bijeljina SJB and the Bijeljina Lower Court. We see underlined in the middle of the page, it's -- there's a confirmation of the SJB Bijeljina of the 19th of June, 1992, of the handing over of the perpetrators to the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is that consistent with your recollection of when these perpetrators were handed over to the military police?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And then there are -- right after that, there are a number of documents referred from the 2000s. There's a 2006 notice of the War Crimes Department of the prosecutor's office. It appears that one of the witnesses was examined in 2004, and there was a decision of the district court in Bijeljina of 2003. And everything else relates to the actions of the Bijeljina police and the Bijeljina Lower Court. So, again, this document confirms that there were no investigative steps taken after this initial investigation until 2003 at the earliest; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just in relation to one of your earlier answers about -- you thought that the military authorities had taken statements or taken some other steps, there's no mention anywhere in this list of evidence that the military authorities took any investigative steps whatsoever. Can you explain that, in light of your earlier answer?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no insight into the documentation of the military authorities, and I could not know what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But on the same page we see several interviews made by SJB Bijeljina. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My point was that there was an investigation conducted by the SJB immediately after this event and this document is consistent with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6219, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now if we could go -- I'm like to move on to another topic, but if we could to P2919, the last page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just before we go to that next topic I'd like to go back briefly to something we discussed yesterday. Yesterday you said that you knew Redzep Sabanovic by sight, and that was at page 35842. So if ... if we could -- if could you have a look at that photo, and if we could make it a bit larger. Are you able to recognise Redzep Sabanovic in this photograph, Mr. Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now then move onto the next topic which is -- in fact the last topic I wanted to discuss with you. And that's the -- your involvement in the commission investigating events in Srebrenica that you discuss at the paragraph 19 of your statement. And you said at that paragraph that you, together with Goran Filipic and Dejan Joksimovic were involved in the commission investigating events surrounding Srebrenica during the war. Now, that commission you refer to, that was the commission formed by the RS government in 2003 that issued its report in June 2004. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I'd just like to make a correction in that explanation of yours. This was a commission that had been established by the government of Republika Srpska, and we, as policemen, tried to establish where the secondary and primary graves were. That was our foremost task in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 24799.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, this is the report that that commission issued in 2004. And the commission members who were listed as signing the report were Milan Bogdanic, Djordje Stojakovic, Smail Cekic, Gordon Bacon, Gojko Vuketic, Milorad Ivosevic, and Zeljko Vujadinovic. So I take it from that that you were not a named commission member but you were working for the commission collecting information; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I had a meeting with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you weren't involved in drafting this report, were you, the actual writing of the report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you were collecting information on behalf of this commission, but I take it you didn't have access to all of the information that this commission gathered from its various sources.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now in your statement you asserted that this report was published under pressure and that it ignored what you referred to as real facts. Now, what this report found was that there was -- there were some combat victims on both sides due to combat between the column fleeing Srebrenica and the VRS and MUP forces. But it also found that VRS and MUP forces detained and executed thousands of Bosnian Muslim males from Srebrenica, and I'd like to take you through some of those findings and ask you some questions about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if, first, we could go to page 14 in the English, page 15 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And here near the top of the page in the English and in the middle of the B/C/S, the report finds that Bosnian Serb MUP forces killed roughly a thousand prisoners at the Kravica warehouse on 13th of July, 1995? Now, is that fact, according to you, true, false, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page 15 of the English and page 16 of the B/C/S. Near the top of the English, near the bottom in the B/C/S, the report concludes that approximately a thousand prisoners from Grbavci were taken away from Grbavci, blindfolded, and executed in meadows in Orahovac, and that around 1500 to 2.000 prisoners whose hands were tied behind their backs were executed at the Petkovci dam, both on the 14th of July. Again is this true, false, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And one more finding at page 18 of the English and page 20 of the B/C/S. Near the top -- at the top of the page in the English and the middle of the B/C/S, the report finds that on the 16th of July, between 1.000 and 1200 prisoners were taken from Pilica and executed at the Branjevo military farm, and around 500 prisoners were executed at the Pilica cultural centre, and another 500 prisoners executed in Kozluk. True, false, or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Again, in your statement, you said that this report was published under pressure and ignored real facts. Can you point to anything specific in this report that you claim is false?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we had a meeting, the entire commission was there, and the meeting was held with the head of the public security centre in Bijeljina, in his office. The commission was so angry at us, they were so rude and brazen that every person had to be found and I immediately saw that all of this was political. This was political pressure from them against us. Really, during that month or two, sometimes we didn't even go home. We established the locations of these primary and secondary graves, and all of that was handed over to them, but during that work, we came to certain facts and evidence that refuted what you presented to us now. That's what I can say. Especially these figures that were bandied about. I'm not challenging that a crime happened but what I'm challenging is that the truth was not established there. That's what I'm saying, actually. As a person who worked in the police for 30 years, that's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you this: Once of the commission's apparent sources of information was Dragan Obrenovic, because there's information in this report discussing Obrenovic's knowledge and actions at this time and I refer to pages 16 and 17. Were you aware of the fact of whether or not Dragan Obrenovic was a source of information for the commission?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We just did police work, that is to say, operative work on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So then you also didn't know that before this report was published, Dragan Obrenovic had pled guilty to and admitted his own involvement in the murder of thousands of Bosnian Muslims from Srebrenica, and had provided a detailed statement of facts about his involvement and the involvement of other VRS and MUP officials and units in these events. That was in May 2003 and that's on the ICTY web site. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And the source of information that you specifically cite in your statement is policeman Meholjic from Srebrenica and what he told you. Now, Mr. Hakija Meholjic was one of the Bosnian Muslim men from Srebrenica who actually made it with the column to ABiH-held territory; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is just one of the many persons that we talked to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But he's the one -- he's the person, the only person you mention in your statement, which is why I ask you about it. So he didn't have any first-hand information about what happened to the men who were detained or captured by the VRS, did he?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since he was a policeman, and I'm a policeman too, it was easiest for me to communicate with him as he talked about how this happened. He didn't say anything specific to me, but he was sort of talking about what had happened. Also, other persons that we talked to indicated that there were something illogical, things that happened and that had not been investigated in accordance with the rules of police work and in accordance with the provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this commission report that's on the screen, the one you criticise and claim was published under pressure, this report was accepted at the time by both the RS government and the RS president, Dragan Cavic, and this was a relatively historic occasion given that it was the first time the RS authorities had acknowledged VRS and MUP responsibility for mass killings in relation to Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a politician and I'm just a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to 65 ter 24801, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may this report be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I was going to seek its admission as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any difficulty. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6220, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I intervene just a moment? Mr. Spasojevic, in answer to the question of Ms. Gustafson, you said you do not challenge that the crimes were committed. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But previously, in -- in answer to the question of Ms. Gustafson regarding the crimes happened at Kravica warehouse, Orahovac, Petkovic, Pilica, Kozluk, et cetera, you said you don't know. What do you mean by saying you do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I know later, but at that moment when it happened I didn't know. That's what I meant when I was answering the Prosecutor's questions. So I know how it happened when we were working on it so that should be in our notes, in the material that is certainly there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now you know what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Spasojevic, on the screen now are conclusions of the RS government from its 99th session held on the 28th of October, 2004, and you can see that under number 1, it says that the government considered and accepted the report of the commission for investigation of events in and around Srebrenica between 10 and 19 July 1995. And if we go to page 3, in both languages, this is part of the explanation attached to the government's conclusions, the document extracts an address that the RS president, Dragan Cavic gave in relation to this report where he stated that the report is the beginning of a difficult and probably for all of us sometimes empty road of disclosing of the truth, and he goes on to talk about the importance of the commission's work and the importance of continuing to walk towards the truth. Now, this document reflects both the fact that the government and president at the time accepted this report and the historic nature of the report and the circumstances; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6221, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to thank you very much, Mr. Spasojevic, for answering my questions so directly and concisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, while we still have this document here before us, can you tell us whether you know who Marko Arsovic is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anyone of these gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know what this means? Due to difficulties that were pointed out in the first preliminary report, the government of Republika Srpska dismissed the chairman of the commission, Mr. Marko Arsovic and appointed Milan Bogdanic as new chairman. Did you know that there was a change there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard about that, but I wasn't that interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, if you didn't know him personally, did you know that Marko Arsovic had been a judge of the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina for many, many years and later on in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that, but I never met him personally. I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 30 in English. I hope it's the same page in Serbian, this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is only four pages. You mean the previous report, Exhibit P6220.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I do apologise. Thank you. 30 in English, please. I believe it's the same in Serbian too. No, it's probably 28 in Serbian then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe it's page 35 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your kindness. Yes, thank you. And we'll also have to move onto 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for this document, as for this report, Mr. Spasojevic, would you sign that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please go back to the previous page in Serbian. Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this, the second paragraph: "There were cases where, in the application, a person is registered as missing in the period of July 1995, but in evidence materials, that date refers to the period before or after July 1995." Did you know that? Is that one of the reasons why you would not sign this document?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's one of the reasons, because these documents were drafted in too amateur a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at this part, there are some persons in four cases, the person represented in the application are still alive. Were there such cases?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D00692. I'm not sure that we have a translation, since it's not there. No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Mr. Meholjic today in answer to the Prosecutor's question there. On the 22nd of April, I think it was last year, I'm not sure, but it must say somewhere, the war-time commander of the Bosnian police in Srebrenica, Hakija Meholjic said at the meeting of the organising board for the celebration of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before reading out, could you put your question, some foundational question first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasojevic, what were the objections about the establishment of facts surrounding Srebrenica in 1995 that you learned from Mr. Meholjic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was more in a conversation that we referred to certain defects there, that there were betrayals and crimes committed within their ranks. Along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you that also the persons who did not perish there were buried?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did refer to several dozen individuals who weren't killed there but who were buried at the memorial centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you enumerate the irregularities that he saw as a policeman of Muslim ethnicity, a fighter for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina, concerning the facts as they were established? Can you list them, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's something that I can say in generalised terms, that he said that he was unhappy, that they had been sold, that they had been sacrificed, that Naser Oric and all the others had fled earlier on, leaving all the wretched and miserable people in the lurch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And as for the establishment effects itself, what were the objections he had and the criticism?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a policeman, he wasn't happy with the way the information was processed, and he said that in ten years time this would come back to haunt us. It was done in an amateurish way and he noted that. He observed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this document now and say whether it reflects what you were told?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the context generally in which it was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If the accused is going to use a document in B/C/S, then he can't just ask a question like that, because otherwise we have no idea what the document says or what's going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. But you are putting the document which we can't read and with a leading question. The answer so adduced has no probative value at all. You are ruining the weight of your evidence, Mr. Karadzic. But he has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasojevic, can I ask you to read, for instance, paragraph 4, where his words are quoted.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, I think we need to back up. We don't even know what this document is. And I think as an initial step, some foundation has to be laid, some questions have to be asked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that Dr. Karadzic can ask him to tell what this document is in general. But I also think in light of the objection and the fact that we can't read it, that asking him to read the pertinent portion is a very useful step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have some foundational fact, but he failed to introduce this as some -- what kind of document it is. That's the first step he should have taken.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I thought that we were familiar with the logo of the news agency by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Spasojevic, who issued this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Republika Srpska news agency "Srna" did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you read for us paragraph 4, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the blood of Srebrenica that the war in BiH was brought to a close. Srebrenica was sold in order for Sarajevo to become a canton. I was in a Srebrenica delegation during the war in 1993, in Sarajevo, at a meeting with Alija Izetbegovic, at which point we rejected his point that Srebrenica be sacrificed in exchange for Vogosca. Unfortunately, this did happen in 1995, and somebody profited from our sacrifices and there was quite a lot of that at the back of the tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read or can you tell us what paragraph 2 says? Can you summarise it for us.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they are -- they have caused us to travel to the ends of the earth while those who remained there squabble over personal interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what about the buried 75 that are mentioned there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those 75 persons who were buried at the memorial centre in Srebrenica whilst not having been killed in Srebrenica should be reburied at an adequate location close by. And as for those who were found to be alive, although their names are on the wall of those that perished at the memorial centre, should be stricken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what else does he say?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that he says that the actual truth about Srebrenica should be told because we know who did what during the war and after the war. What he meant was that the victims should not be the subject of manipulation or offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how does this concord with what he told you when you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we spoke, he told me the same story although in what were police terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Spasojevic -- just a second. You said that this is what "Srna" issued. But is this an interview or -- or a news report by a journalist, or what? What -- what is it about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I'm seeing it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasojevic, can you look at paragraph 1. What is this about, what sort of report and about which meeting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is some sort of organising committee that is charged with marking the 11th of July, organised by the families of the victims. That's something that Hamdija Meholjic must have said on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, it's a news report from that meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this is just an example. The title of the document on e-court says it's Meholjic's statement and what we all can see is "Srna." And we have no idea what this document is about. Whether alleged Mr. Meholjic wrote an article or statement under the title of "Srna." So you should introduce some foundation before you put the question. Not only the content. Can I hear from you, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't have anything to add. I think my objections were all along the same lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D3143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies for my inartfulness. I thought it was clear that this was a news report about a meeting and I wanted to save time. At any rate, I kindly ask for your understanding in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasojevic, you stated today that everything you did was noted down in records that exist. And where should they be?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they should be in public security centre in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, how can we search for it in the archives? Is there a title that this collection of documents would have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be listed under the Srebrenica case. That's how it would be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You spoke about gathering information. As a policeman, in order to establish facts, was it important for you to read the statements of Dragan Obrenovic and others?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While working on this case, did you come across a fact that would speak about my involvement in the activities following the fall of Srebrenica that you described?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 14, you were asked why it was that between 1992 and 2003, no investigations were conducted. My question for you is this: Is it necessary for the activities that a certain body charged with investigation carried out contemporaneously to be re-done at a later point?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At page 12, line 20, my learned friend Ms. Gustafson said that they were set free. They were released. Were they, indeed, released, and was this case closed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they spent some 20 days in military detention. At the time, the military court was being set up, possibly there were no conditions in place, and it is possible that statements were taken from them and that they were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would the case have been closed or would it have remained open and then on the basis of that case, a trial followed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was on the basis of that case file, on the basis of -- that our documentation, the court in Belgrade conducted proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The investigation material cites Dosa Todorovic as one of the victims. Can you tell the Chamber who she is, if you know, and specifically what her ethnicity is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She's a disabled woman who lives on her own, and she's a Serb. They took her money and jewellery, and I think they killed her. I can't recall at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, a Serb lady was robbed, and this was part of that same crime; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday at page 97, you were asked about the investigation concerning those other cases, those other families. Can you tell us this: As the investigation was in course, how were the perpetrators listed, as known or unknown?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as unknown. We knew nothing of them. This event was something that became public knowledge three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You mean these events --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I learnt of those events three days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when were the perpetrators finally identified?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't set a specific time on that. It was something that was at the forefront of our minds. This case was open, it was a crime, but I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Going back to what I asked you earlier on, the case involving Dosa Todorovic and Muslims. Was it the case that the state suppressed some information or failed to do anything in that respect?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it was a case like any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What sort of role could the president of the republic have played in the activities carried out by investigative and judicial bodies?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what became of this individual Malovic who was mentioned as a possible perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed in Belgrade. I don't know which year that was, but that was shortly after the events. Apparently he was involved in heroin smuggling together with another Belgrade criminal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In connection with the events in 1992, March and April, you said that you yourself saw the body of one Stevanovic. Can you tell us what his ethnicity was and whether he was a soldier or a civilian?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was close to the building where I live. This civilian, Stevanovic, I believe he was a Serb. I don't know. I don't know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 89 - that was yesterday - you were also asked about victims, and probably because of the linguistic nuances, the matter remained unclear. Mr. Spasojevic, do you distinguish between the term "killed," as in murdered, and killed as in got killed? And if you do distinguish between these terms, in what way do you do so?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, murdered means the person is dead, of course. But you have to establish how death came about. And killed, of course, is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, please continue. Put a pause between the questions and the answers. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do we call the victims who lost their lives in combat and how do we call the victims who lost their lives because of a criminal murder? How would you call one and how would you call the other?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, victims are those who get killed in armed conflict. And we also have victims of crime who were murdered. Someone took their life. And it was an act. I did not add this in my statement. Their intention was to loot Ramovic, but it was unfortunate that one of them killed him because he was more intoxicated than the other one. I just don't know which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have already moved to 1992, Stevanovic, and you said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. In your answer, we heard same terminology of "victims." Did you distinguish in B/C/S? Victims of those who get killed in armed conflict and the victims of crime? We heard the same term, "victims." But did you use different terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is similar. Similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a victim of an armed conflict was someone who lost his life, and you have a criminal act when somebody takes somebody's life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How do you spell a victim of an armed conflict in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That also means that someone's life was taken. But in the other case, the victim's life was also taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The spelling is the same in -- in both cases. You use the same term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In armed conflict, you would say a victim of armed conflict. And if it's a criminal act, a criminal offence, then we talk about victims who were murdered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about the words "ubijen," killed, and "poginuo," also killed. Who are the persons that we say are "poginuli" and who are the persons we say are "ubijeni"?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Ubijeni," killed, in one sense is when he and the other side also used weapons. And "poginuo" is killed -- means sporadically, by a stray bullet or between two -- caught by cross-fire and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday on page 90 you said that doctors examined the bodies. Was it the so-called external examination or do you know whether in those who were victims of conflict forensic analysis was done or autopsies? Or were these victims considered victims of armed conflicts or victims of murder in the criminal sense?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We consider them to be victims of armed conflict. And in Bijeljina we do not have an autopsy expert. This is why only an external examination of the bodies was conducted by the doctors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is described somewhere; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The documents exist and they should be available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have a look at the photograph, P2919. Page 28, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look closely at the position of the arms and head. And can you tell us whether these persons are alive or dead and whether it is possible that they were ordered to lie down facing the pavement. Please look at the arms under the head in one and the other case.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the first one has this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The latter part of this question, I think, just calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to hear the answer. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first person lying down, there seems to be a pool of blood. There's some liquid there and it seems to me that it's blood. And as for the other two persons, at a first glance, as a layman, I perhaps would think that they are alive because they have their arms put in front of their heads. But it's difficult to judge only on the basis of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recognise the persons and the area? Could you tell us where this was shot?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not familiar. It seems to be a back street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you said that Arkan arrived with 16 men. Could you tell us how many Arkan's men were killed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that. I learned this information only afterwards, after the termination of the armed conflict, that there were around 15 or 16 of them, but I don't know how many lost their lives. That's really interesting. Because I didn't do this. It was a colleague of mine who conducted the external examination of the bodies and so on, and therefore I couldn't really tell you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Please tell us though, you did mention something about it, but just tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's now time for me to put a question to you. But putting that question, I will have to ask you whether it is your case that the -- these persons are alive being ordered to lie down facing the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's our case that we don't know. And nor has it been proven that these people are deceased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you challenge the evidence that the lady was the one who we saw in another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't stipulate to that evidence, so we put the Prosecution to their proof on all of these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Spasojevic, could you tell us, as you told us that most barricades were located around the police building, can you tell us where there were most Muslim casualties on the 31st of March and the 1st of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was near the hospital, in the direction of Zvornik. It's one -- that was the town hospital, and that was where the biggest barricade was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Spasojevic. Thank you for your testimony -- thank you for -- oh, excuse me. Who did you do this for, all these activities that you carried out and applying the law?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've been a policeman since 1976 and I did as I was taught to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any obstructions or pressure from government organs or any requests to turn a blind eye to something, to cover something up?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SPASOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for having come here to testify and for having been a good policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Spasojevic. On behalf of the Chamber, I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. We'll rise all together. We'll break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First I'd like to introduce Nabilah Reza, from Australia, who is one of our legal interns who will be joining us for this session. We've managed to get all of our interns into court this week and take advantage of the absence of Mr. Sladojevic, but he'll be back on Monday. With respect to the next witness, Mr. President, I wanted to address one issue in private session, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I only want to correct one small matter. On the 19th of March, 2013, the -- Dr. Karadzic filed a revised 92 ter notification for this witness, and it's actually the first and only 92 ter notification that we got. It's not a revised one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ljubojevic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Mr. Ljubojevic, I take it you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Ljubojevic, I must draw your attention to a certain Rule of Procedure and Evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal. That is, Rule 90(E). Under this Rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges, if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you, and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But, in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in -- compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Ljubojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ljubojevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I will ask you to speak slowly and so will I also have to do so that everything will be recorded. We also should make pauses between question and answer so that everything would be interpreted.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show up 1D7945 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see your statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please just make slightly longer pauses between you -- providing your answers. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the last page please be shown to the witness so that he would identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully convey what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to my best recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions, would your answers be substantially the same as those given in this statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement in accordance with 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3144, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read the summary of Mr. Dragomir Ljubojevic's statement in the English language. [In English] Dragomir Ljubojevic was born on 18th of November, 1951, in Velika Obarska village, Bijeljina municipality, where he still resides. He was the manager of the Elvako plant in Bijeljina when activities of the Muslim union members of the plant began to create ethnic tensions in the entire municipality. Until this point, when the SDA and HDZ formed and openly strove for separatism in their political programmes and activities, relations between different ethnic groups in the municipality had been good. The Muslim workers that went on strike in the Elvako plant did so with purely political demands; they wanted the factory management to be exclusively Muslim. These activities were encouraged by the SDA who provided food for workers in the part of the factory under blockade. These activities continued to the centre of the town, where other local institutions were also blockaded. This impeded the functioning of the local government, and after repeated refusal of the strikers to negotiate, the MUP was forced to put down the demonstrations and lift the blockade of government institutions. Mr. Dragomir Ljubojevic believes that the Muslim leadership in Bijeljina agitated these tensions in order to provide more fertile ground for their separatist political aims. Meanwhile, Serbs and a small number of Muslims carried out the obligations stipulated by law and the constitution and participated in the mobilisation of the JNA units. The majority of Muslims, however, avoided mobilisation, and some joined the paramilitary forces in Croatia and fought against those same JNA units and the Serbs in Croatia. The Serb population felt much anxiety and fear at these events, particularly in the context of the atrocities committed against Serbs during the Second World War. Dragomir Ljubojevic responded to mobilisation and was sent to the Brcko general sector on 3rd of May, 1992, where he was tasked with lifting the blockade established by armed civilians and paramilitary formations. He was seriously wounded there and on sick-leave until June the 6th, 1993. This makes the allegation that Dragomir Ljubojevic organised the alleged expulsion of Muslims in November 1992 impossible. Dragomir Ljubojevic was elected president of the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly. During his duties at the municipal assembly, Dragomir Ljubojevic did not come across a single decision made by the Crisis Staff. Any decisions made by the War Presidency were fully transparent and published in the bulletin accessible to the public. During this period, the local municipal leadership worked to normalise life, displaced persons were returned, property returned to them, mosques rebuilt, and refugees provided with accommodations. President Karadzic insisted to Dragomir Ljubojevic that the local government exert maximum care for displaced persons and refugees regardless of their religion or nationality and to promote peaceful co-existence of Muslims and Serbs. Dragomir Ljubojevic was never ordered to plan or execute any expulsion of the non-Serbs from Bijeljina municipality, nor did Dragomir Ljubojevic give such orders to any subordinates. Those who left did so voluntarily in the hope of finding a better situation elsewhere. On the other hand, Dragomir Ljubojevic estimates that nearly 400.000 expelled and deported Serbs passed through Bijeljina in the course of the war. By 1995, more than 50.000 Serb refugees were accommodated in Bijeljina from parts of BH under the control of BH army. The circumstances of the people passing through Bijeljina were very desperate, as these people had by now lived through four years of war. And that is a short summary. At that moment, I do not have questions for Mr. Ljubojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ljubojevic, as you have noted, your evidence in-chief in this case has been admitted in writing in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ljubojevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me first thank you again for participating in an interview with the Prosecution on the 20th of March, 2013, that is, on Wednesday. I just want to sum up a few statements that you made during this interview. You said that you did not know that Arkan had a training camp in Badovinci and that young men were sent there for training by the SDS. That's right, that's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that I did not know that this camp existed and that I was not aware that anyone was sending young men there for training.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I actually had just said, and I just wanted you to confirm that you said that. Maybe the translation was saying something different.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You also said that you got only aware of Arkan being present in Bijeljina after the fighting broke out; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to Arkan's activities, you only -- you said that you would only know from stories that he had a football fan club and that he had been active in Croatia during the war. That's what you said; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: If you remember, you asked me whether before these things happened in Bijeljina I had known Arkan. I said that before the war, I had heard of him and thereby knew of him as the leader of the Red Star football club fans and that before that, I had no contact with him. I never encountered him, never came across him even during the Bijeljina war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ljubojevic, when I asked you about the murder of the Sarajlic family in summer 1992, you said that you heard about this incident but you would not know who did it and why the murders -- murder was committed; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that everybody in the municipality of Bijeljina condemned that killing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you were told that Vojvoda Mirko Blagojevic claimed in a public announcement that his family -- that this family was murdered by a special police unit, you said that you would not know this, but perhaps Mr. Blagojevic had more information about this than you had. That's what you said; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I agree, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, when I asked you whether you know that the Muslim commander Halilovic, a member of the VRS, was expelled from Bijeljina, you said that you had heard that but that you would not know the details; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when I asked you whether you know that Vojkan Jokovic was made responsible for this expulsion and that there was evidence before this Court that he expelled non-Serbs unwilling to leave, you said that you would not know that but you wouldn't exclude it either; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But you said Vojkan Jokovic and it should be Djurkovic. All the rest is correct, exactly the way I had said it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to Vojkan Djurkovic, you mentioned during the interview that he came from a village near Bijeljina and he was one of Arkan's men; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I would see him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
