utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, you explained that you were seriously wounded on the 4th of May, 1992, while involved in de-blockading the hospital in Brcko and that you subsequently was treated in the Bijeljina hospital until 23rd of May and then released into house care. That is correct, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because there wasn't enough room in hospital for longer recuperation because the wounded from the Tuzla column were more urgent cases than I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in paragraph 8 of your statement, you state that from the 6th of June, 1993, until 1994, you were in the 2nd Semberija Light Infantry Brigade. And in the interview on Wednesday, you said that Mr. Filipovic was your superior and the commander of the brigade was Blagoje Gavrilovic, who was initially the commander of a JNA reconnaissance group; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As to your deployment in the VRS, you said during the interview that you were on the front line in Brcko and that, depending on the front-line activities, you were able to return home at night, but, of course, not all nights, and that the regular shift was seven days front-line duty and then seven days rest at home. That's -- sums it up; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the way it usually was for combatants who fought in the trenches but not for the auxiliary services. It is correct as regards the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, during the interview on Wednesday, you said that you did not have a function in the SDS. You were a member but not a functionary. You were only on a list for deputies of the Bijeljina Assembly and in fact became a member of --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Assemblyman.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. But you became a member of the Bijeljina Assembly only by the end of 1992, beginning 1993, and that at that time the Assembly didn't really function; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Presidency carried out the duties of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just to confirm, you only became president of the -- of the -- of Bijeljina Assembly in 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. January 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will concentrate in this cross-examination on the period before you were wounded. And you said in paragraph 11 of your statement that you do not know that there was a Crisis Staff in Bijeljina and that you only know that there was a War Presidency. And, in this context, I want to show you P02629.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can this be on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up - and you will see it soon hopefully - it's a note by the Bijeljina chief -- SJB chief Jesuric to the minister of interior on the situation in Bijeljina in April 1992. It's a bit hard to read the -- the B/C/S. Therefore, I -- I read from the first page of -- of this -- of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the English, it's the last paragraph and starting there, and then turning further to the next page. And in the B/C/S, if you look at the -- the page 2, B/C/S page 2 -- oh, sorry, page 3. Next page. It's the paragraphs 2 and 3. And Mr. Jesuric refers here to the barricades on the 31st of March, 1991, and then he states: "During the night and the next day, the TO, the Serbian National Guard and the Serbian Volunteer Guard started removing the barricades under the supervision of the Bijeljina Municipal Assembly Crisis Staff." We need to move to the next page in the English. And in the middle of the next paragraph, there's reference to -- the Bijeljina Crisis Staff is again mentioned, in relation to schools.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, you were not aware of this Crisis Staff that Mr. Jesuric mentions here being obviously in charge of both military and civilian matters?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, also most recently here in court --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I refer here, Your Honour, to P05587.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- we reviewed an interview that Ms. Plavsic gave when she visited Bijeljina on the 4th of April, 1992, in a delegation. And in that interview, she also makes a reference that she left that delegation she came with to see -- to come to see the Crisis Staff first. Mr. Ljubojevic, Ms. Plavsic is aware of a Crisis Staff in Bijeljina and met it, but you, who are actually active in politics in Bijeljina at the time, you were not. How can that be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: It is possible there were Crisis Staffs in some municipalities. But I claim with full responsibility that in the municipality of Bijeljina there was no Crisis Staff and that the Presidency functioned throughout, in the municipality of Bijeljina. So, as is well known, the Serbs were a majority in the municipality of Bijeljina and all posts were held by Serbs, except for these few, so the Territorial Defence, the Civil Protection and the Presidency were the authorities in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have D01585 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, you will see it's a handwritten document by the SDS Municipal Board to the SDS Main Board dated 3rd of April, 1992. Mr. Kojic, you know him and his function, right, as the president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Savo Kojic refers here in this short document to the decision of the SAO Semberija and Majevica Crisis Staff and the Serbian National Guard commander. So he also speaks about the Crisis Staff. He calls it here the SAO Semberija and Majevica Crisis Staff. You're not aware of that either?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that this document is not right because the SAO Semberija did not have any functions, organs, and could not have had a Crisis Staff. I don't know what the motive was of Mr. Kojic, and I don't know whether this is really his letter. I cannot comment upon that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in this letter, there's also the reference to the Serbian National Guard commanders. The Serbian National Guard commander, that was Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. In April, he certainly wasn't commander of the Guard that was not there, this unit that was commanded by Mr. Savic. In April, on the 3rd of April, there certainly was no Guard that was commanded by Mr. Savic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is, to your recollection, the date when there was this Guard commanded by Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer? Where would you put it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: It is the beginning of May. I think the Guard was established on the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mauzer's Guard was a sort of SDS -- sorry. And Mauzer's Guard was sort of SDS army, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. It was a unit of the Army of Republika Srpska. And it was never a party army. It consisted of persons that came from all areas, from different areas and the area of Bijeljina itself, the local population.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have P02855 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's a military document, Mr. Ljubojevic. It's a report of the 1st Krajina Corps Command to the VRS Main Staff dated the 28th of July, 1992, about paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And -- and we need page 5 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you look in the middle, in the middle of the document, there is a description of the Serbian National Guard in Bijeljina, and it says here: "The Serbian National Guard in Bijeljina has formally joined the so-called special brigade. The Serbian National Guard was formed by the Bijeljina SDS, and the Presidency of the Bijeljina Municipality Assembly decided that this would be the army of Bijeljina which would defend Bijeljina should it be attacked, and appointed self-styled Major Ljubisa Savic, Mauzer, as the [sic] commander." Mr. Ljubojevic, that would be a correct description by Colonel Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that there are many mistakes there and that Colonel Tolimir was misinformed. The unit had not been established by the SDS. That is the first mistake. This was a unit that had been established by the staff of the Territorial Defence. And that it was the municipality of Bijeljina that stood behind this, that is correct. And it is correct that Ljubisa Savic was the first commander, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the interview with me, you said that Mauzer was integrated in the VRS, Mauzer and the Guards were integrated in the VRS and a commander of an elite unit --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Immediately upon its establishment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And you said that it was an elite unit that took part in offensive operations on the front line; correct? That's --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also said that Mr. Savic and his men functioned as an escort to Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik when they visited Bijeljina. That's what you said; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said and that was not discussed. Who escorted Mr. Karadzic when he came, I really don't know. If they were, then that pertained to the knowledge of superior commands. This was certainly done -- not done in an arbitrary fashion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yesterday here in court - and, Your Honours, I refer here to T35808 - a witness stated that the Presidency of the municipality of Bijeljina appointed Blagoje Gavrilovic, Zivan Filipovic and Vasilije Andric as the corps of the command of the TO of Bijeljina in the early days; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: If someone who is competent and who has valid documents said that, then I agree. I am not aware of that detail about the appointment and who was appointed to which particular position, but I do know that the Presidency performed its function and that it was able to appoint the mentioned gentlemen to some of these positions of responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the Presidency at the time, which persons were that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the names exactly, but I do know that it is the president of the Assembly that presides and the chief of the Territorial Defence, and there are other functions that were important for the normal functioning of the municipality and all institutions, both in the municipality and on the ground.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Transcript. The witness said "ex officio" and that was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the president of the Assembly, the president of the municipal government called the president of the Executive Board at the time, and the other members.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, in paragraph 8, you describe that you went to Brcko on the 3rd of May, 1992, as a member of the TO. And you -- during the interview, you also described that you were present on the square in Bijeljina when Mauzer addressed those present with a megaphone, and that you were in that convoy of buses moving to Brcko and that among the soldiers were Mauzer's Guard, Gavrilo's men and Vojvoda Blagojevic with his men; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were all there and the units of the Territorial Defence, they were all under the command of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Brcko Crisis Staff had actually asked the Bijeljina authorities for help?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will move now onto another topic. In paragraph 12 of your statement, you describe how Bijeljina was a refuge for many Serbian refugees and you go into a great many details of the arrival of huge numbers of Serbs from the -- throughout the period 1991 through 1995. There had to be housing and means for this huge amount of homeless Serbs, right, and --

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Displaced persons had to be put up. Since Bijeljina is a municipality on the border, it had the ability to provide enough food because we are an agricultural area and that motivated people to come to Bijeljina. When they were in Bijeljina, we had no choice because these unfortunate persons had to leave their homes and we had to take care of them up until that moment when they would find a better solution, to go to Serbia or to go abroad. Many stayed in Bijeljina, and we had a situation whereby there would even be more than 50.000 persons in Bijeljina along with 60.000 local inhabitants, Serbs, and 10.000 Bosniaks who lived in the municipality of Bijeljina throughout.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And room was made in homes and other means be provided by expelling Muslims. Isn't that how it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Surplus housing was taken from everyone, Serbs and Bosniaks. For example, in town and in the villages that are primarily Serb populated, an enormous amount of displaced persons were put up in Serb homes. So it's not correct that displaced persons were only put up in Bosniak houses. All of Semberija provided refuge to these unfortunate persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have document P05483 be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as it is coming up, it is a press communication -- and we only have it in English, Mr. Ljubojevic. It's a press communication of the Red Cross about the expulsion of 432 Muslims in the night of the 28th of August, 1994, from Bijeljina, that were forced by the Bosnian Serb authorities to cross the front line into Bosnian government-held territory near Tuzla, and they state here in this communication that it is the eighth transport of that kind. Most of them, women, children, the elderly, and the sick. "They were forcibly taken from their homes and stripped of their belongings, and, in addition, they had to pay a large amount of money for their transport." Mr. Ljubojevic, you must be aware of this. It's not a single incident. It's a pattern, is it not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that that report is not correct. And I'm not aware of that having happened, so I have to put a self-defeating fact to you that some representatives of the international community who were in certain areas, to the best of my knowledge, wrote dramatic reports in order to keep their own positions, the positions that they acquired by being accredited somewhere. They were partial and they were not well-intentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This pattern of expulsion that the ICRC describe here, we heard from witnesses - and I want to refer here to Mr. Davidovic, Your Honours, it's P02848, paragraph 70 - that this was widely known in Bijeljina that this was happening, and he was a man living there. So how could you not have heard it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic was a policeman. If he knew that, then it was a fault of his that he failed to prevent this. He was not an ordinary citizen. If he knew and failed to prevent it, then this is a sin that should be apportioned to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's go briefly also back again to this -- to this communication. There is also a mention in this communication, a reference to military-aged men being arrested and many of them forced to join work units often deployed near the front line. Mr. Ljubojevic, such men were detained in Batkovic camp, were they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of these details.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And while you were on the front line, were such detainees not also used at your section of the front line for deployment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, we had no need of that. Our members were mostly farmers and workers, and they didn't find it difficult to make their lines, to maintain their defence lines, and to man them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Sorry to intervene Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. By Mr. Davidovic you meant Milorad Davidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He described this praxis in his written evidence at paragraph 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, could you expand again to me what his fault was with respect to what Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I presume that Mr. Davidovic, being a policeman, had ways and means to learn certain events and to -- to prevent them. Or to inform someone that something of the sort was going on and who were those who were conducting themselves dishonourably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where was he living at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suppose that he was in Bijeljina. He is a native of Bijeljina, and I assume - I don't know - because if he said that he was aware of it, then he must have been present in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Back to you Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just to clarify one matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, Mr. Davidovic was in the federal SUP in Belgrade deployed and not as a police officer in Bijeljina. So the police officers in Bijeljina should have stopped what was going on, should they not?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Up until the 15th of May, or through to the end of May, the powers of federal organs extended to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know what the date was when these federal powers ceased, but I do know that the police respected what the federal organs had to say, and this was true for the other organs as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, by that time, Yugoslavia, the former Yugoslavia, didn't exist anymore. There was only Serbia and Montenegro in Yugoslavia at that time, so how could they possibly intervene in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I said that he could find ways and means of officially informing someone about the information he had. It is a pity, really, that we don't have a document which would say when this happened and who these people were. Then we could give comments of a more pertinent nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, we just have here this ICRC communication, and it's the 28th of August and they speak about obviously August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have P02932 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you will see, when it comes up, it is another press communication of the Red Cross about ethnic cleansing in Bijeljina, and it's now September 1994. And they refer -- the ICRC refers here to more than 2.500 Muslims being cleansed from Bijeljina. So that's a huge amount of people, and so how can you not have been aware this? And the local police.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Please. The movements that occurred of the population oftentimes happened with -- in keeping with the wishes of the Muslims. We must bear in mind that in Bijeljina at that time there were 50.000 people who had been forced to leave their homes. The situation was complex and very sensitive. In confined space, we had also people who had lost their nearest and dearest. We had the wounded. Bijeljina was an area where life was hard. Even those who were locals had a hard time living in Bijeljina at the time. You have to bear in mind the fact that this was a humane resettlement of people. People wanted to move to an area where they felt that they would have a better life. Many of those people went to Western countries where they remain today -- to date. Their properties remained behind. They are still owners of the property, and they can enjoy their property today. It cannot be qualified the way you just did. At that time, it may have appeared this way, but today we certainly have much more information that would portray to us what the events were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript recorded only poorly what the witness said. Can the witness speak more slowly. The witness said that they reported to be taken elsewhere, and this wasn't recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My last document, just one more document, and it is P03862. And it's, again, a -- a document only in the English language. It is a code cable from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan from 15 September 1994. Can -- can we have the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you look at the reference number 7, reference is made to the expulsion in Bijeljina. It's now the UN. And there is also a reference that Mr. Karadzic has stated that an investigation was initiated in the role of Major Vojkan Djurkovic in this. You -- you see that. There is a reference to Vojkan Djurkovic and that Mr. Karadzic had stated that an investigation was initiated. Do you know about this investigations again -- against Djurkovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, no. When I took up my duties in January of 1996, there was talk that a proceedings had been initiated against Mr. Djurkovic in order to establish the facts of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he ever convicted, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, my time is up. No further questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Do you have any re-examination, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly, Your Excellency, just a number of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Today, at page 56, it was suggested, it was read out from a text or a suggestion was made in the question to the effect that 420 Muslims had been driven out of Bijeljina in 1994 by the authorities. Can you tell us, what part did the authorities play in the moving out of the population, and what was their position with regard to the activities of this one Vojkan?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The authorities in Bijeljina tried throughout that time to create conditions so that people in Bijeljina could live normally. As for Mr. Djurkovic's actions, the authorities did not view them favourably and did not approve of this way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To the best of your knowledge, at the time you were an assemblyman and not the president of the municipality, this view that the authorities had driven these people out, would that, in your mind, be correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. That is absolutely not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. -- was Mr. Davidovic ever a policeman in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Davidovic intervened in 1990 when the workers of the Elvako company went on strike. But he was a policeman in Bijeljina for a while before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Davidovic went to work for the federal SUP, did he appear in Bijeljina, Brcko and Zvornik, and, if so, in what capacity?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have an occasion to meet Mr. Davidovic in that period of time. However, according to the information I received, his intervention in the municipality of Zvornik was well known. At that point, he intervened against a paramilitary unit or something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 57, an allegation was made that the Muslims had some sort of compulsory work service that they had to do. Were the Muslims under a military duty of conscription and were they forced to join the ranks of the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were not forced. But there was a number of Muslims who voluntarily joined the ranks of -- of the Republika Srpska army. I know for a fact that in the 3rd Semberija Brigade, there was a battalion of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This compulsory work service, did it apply only to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. All those who were not fit for military service or had to remain at their workplace because of the nature of the work they discharged were under compulsory work service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Serbs or Muslims or altogether all of them who were under compulsory work service, were they put up in some quarters at the end of their workday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they had the possibility of returning home after a day's work, unless there were any other problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 50, you were shown that there was a -- a Crisis Staff of SAO Semberija and Majevica. Previously you were asked whether the municipality, as such, had its Crisis Staff. Did you, at any point, before assuming your position, come across a single document of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Even the document that was shown to me just now was one that I have seen for the first time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 47, you said that you were released for -- to -- for medical treatment at home because there was no room in the hospital because of the Tuzla column. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was wounded on the 4th of May, I was seriously wounded. And then on the 15th of May, following the massacre which was committed in Brcanska Malta at Tuzla, a number of these seriously wounded individuals were transported to Bijeljina. They were put up elsewhere, as well. However, a large number of those who were transported to Bijeljina were hospitalised there. They were given medical treatment. Some underwent surgeries. Others were forwarded to hospitals in Belgrade. There were a great many seriously wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And, lastly, at page 47, you were asked about the departure of Mr. Halilovic who was not willing to leave. Can you tell us what Mr. Halilovic was doing in Bijeljina during the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Halilovic was the commander of a unit that was manned by Muslims, that consisted of Muslims. He was otherwise employed in the Duhan or the tobacco company in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The authorities and the high officials, deputies, party members, how did they react to this forcible departure of Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: There was utter astonishment and disapproval of this act, and ways were sought to assist the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether some of those who were included in these transfers were ever allowed to come back at their request?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you have anything else to say about your knowledge of my position vis-a-vis the war and humanitarian issues, specifically the ones we've been discussing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, distinguished Prosecution, I have to say that, thanks to the fact that he headed the Serbian people, and I mean President Karadzic, as an honourable man, humanist, legalist, many misfortunes were averted. It is truly a pity that, at that time, in Bosnia, there wasn't another such patriot and statesman who would have been his interlocutor and partner in the resolution of these complex issues. Certainly had that been the case, Bosnia would have been a much more happier and prosperous state in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 01293. Also the telegrams of the United Nations dated September 1994. I will read out a few in English. I mean, read out a few passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's see how Mr. Akashi communicated with me on this issue. The first paragraph reads: "[In English] As outlined in my Z-1279 of 20th of August, 1994, I raised with Dr. Karadzic at our last meeting in Pale the ongoing abuses of human rights around Bijeljina. At that time, Dr. Karadzic attributed the problem to criminals and undertook to replace the chief of police due to what he acknowledged was a very unsatisfactory situation in the area with respect to security and crime. "I have subsequently learned that the chief of police has been indeed replaced." [Interpretation] And so on. How does this tally with your knowledge of the fact that the authorities were aware of the fact that this was done by criminals and that the chief of police was replaced? Not because he had done anything but because he was unable to contain them or prevent them from doing what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: What was well known, for sure, was that you, as the president, and the government, complete with municipal structures, always tried to create a climate that would allow people to live normally. And this was an environment that was very difficult to reckon with, in terms of security and politically, to find a solution for all the people in Bijeljina and beyond to leave peacefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your question should have stopped with question mark. The latter part is very much leading or feeding. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise for my lack of skill, and, trust me, it is not deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that he received information that it was -- and let me read it to you from the fourth paragraph: "[In English] Many of those who have been expelled have reported the systematic practice of forced labour in the areas from which they have arrived, as well as other severe human rights violations, including torture" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Do we have it --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- "rape and sexual assaults" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably next page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I asked for the next page to be shown. Fourth paragraph, please. This is a statement for the press mentioned on the previous page by His Excellency Mr. Akashi. And he says: "[In English] Many of those who have been expelled have reported the systematic practice of forced labour in the areas from which they have arrived, as well as other severe human rights violations, including torture, rape and sexual assault, arbitrary arrest and detention, and arbitrary deprivation of property."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this what those who crossed over to the Muslim side told and reported correct? Was it correct? Let me start with the last. Was property seized from anyone and the ownership changed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was a commission which made lists of property. They listed the property, and the property was assigned for use to some of the displaced persons; but after the war, it was returned to previous owners as it is only proper. I have to say that the property-related issues and the property-related problems were best resolved in Bijeljina in all of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And what is not true about this is that it's a fact that there were instances of abuse. In addition to all these problems and a huge number of domestic population and displaced persons, Bijeljina was certainly the safest town in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any instances of torture, rape, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's move onto another topic. I doubt that this is arising from the line of cross-examination. But because in the document, I just let the first question be asked. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, but I would argue that the cross-examination raised the issue of reports that had been received by the international community concerning events in Bijeljina, and if those reports can be shown to have been untrue or exaggerated, it seems to be within the scope of the cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see no problem with it. But the content, subject matter, Mr. Karadzic just dealt with was related to a totally separate matter. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the next page, please, from the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a letter which the High Commissioner for Refugees wrote to me on the 5th of September. And he says the following, that: "1300 members of minority communities in Bijeljina and Janja area have been forced to leave their homes by your authorities and expelled towards Tuzla." He says further on that the situation is similar in Banja Luka. And he continues: "[In English] [As read] The expulsions from the Bijeljina area are combined with the exaction of significant sums of money reportedly by a man known as Vojkan and take place in circumstances that create great hardship for, and sometimes" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's what I was wondering. It is starting as an UN document but now there is something else. Mr. Reid is just checking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think this has been admitted separately as a public exhibit. But Mr. Reid would be better placed ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me check the -- what's the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I don't know the exhibit number, but I think -- if we can check, I think it may have been admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we just found out it's public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, this is a UN document, because it's the commission, that is to say, an agency of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So when it is said about the Bijeljina authorities that in this month, that is to say, in September, 1300 Muslims were expelled from Bijeljina and Janja and Vojkan is mentioned in relation with that, can you tell us what is true of everything that these people were told? Was that the number of people who were expelled? Were they expelled or not? Was it done by the authorities? And was Vojkan an exponent of the authorities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: As I said in the very beginning, the authorities in Bijeljina were never involved with this issue in such a way that they would strip someone of his right to reside there, have property, or work. What was a major problem in Bijeljina was a lack of living space, and in such a situation, many people decided to leave Bijeljina. And a number of Bosniaks left Bijeljina, but I have to say that certainly several thousand local people left Bijeljina too, whole families or parts of families. So this cannot only refer to the Bosniaks. It can be checked in various records that whole families of Serbs, that is to say, the domestic population, left throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina and also throughout Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the first two documents can be considered one and the same, 01293, the first two pages, if it's has not been admitted, then I would tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The first two pages will be Exhibit D3145, and the third page is Exhibit P2087.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: D3145. And the next --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the third page is actually Exhibit P2087.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And both of them were admitted publicly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. On the 14th of January, 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The last question, Mr. Ljubojevic. According to your knowledge, what was the accuracy of media reports as well as the reports of the people who crossed over to the other side? Did you establish, and did you have any knowledge about the degree of trust one could put in that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Reports were sensationalist --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's now very leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. That's very general. But -- could you reformulate your question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Having seen these allegations, the statement of Ambassador Akashi refers to what people who crossed there said. Based on that, what can you tell us about the degree of accuracy? How reliable was the information that those who crossed to the other side would divulge there, and how, in what way, did you assess media reports concerning events that were aware of? How were they represented in the media?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything was dramatised --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see any improvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't see that that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It could have been better if he would have stopped after the first question mark. But it's the same point basically made -- maybe being made two times. But it's not leading. He is not suggesting an answer, and I think the witness is capable of answering it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with your observation. He could or should have stopped with the first question mark. The next part is sort of leading to a certain extent. So could you put your question again, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, with regard to the events that you were familiar with, what was the accuracy of the reports given by people who crossed to the other side and also reports of the media? How were the events represented in the media?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: The media dramatised all events. People who came, people who left, certainly told fantastical stories in order to reinforce their position there. This is well known. And what is most important, the story provided by representatives of international organisations always favoured the stories about the trials and tribulations of the Muslims, and as for those who arrived to Bijeljina, no one reported about their problems. We could not see that in the reports that we could see. But everything was dramatised more than was realistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us about what did you mean about those who were arriving in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, in Bijeljina, all buildings and property have been preserved. We have a situation that some figures and some dates are mentioned here when people from around Tuzla came to Bijeljina from places which had been razed to the ground and their property torched. That did not happen in Bijeljina. The problem in Bijeljina throughout the war was that all of the property was saved by contrast to Smoluca and other places.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the names of villages.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Especially those in Central Bosnia that people came from where their property had been completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the names of the places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ljubojevic, you seem to speak a bit too fast. It is very difficult to -- for the interpreters to catch up with your speed. Could you kindly repeat all the names of municipalities or places.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I always get carried away when I talk about these events and issues. In the vicinity of Tuzla, from which, in a period, the number of displaced persons coming was the greatest, the following populated places, Pozarnica, Sinin Han, Smoluca, Potpec, were torched and other places too, especially in Central Bosnia, from which many expellees arrived in Bijeljina. And what is particularly important and what discredits these reports to a degree as well is that they only discuss the problems that the Muslims were facing, and they could have obtained information about the state of property of those who had arrived in Bijeljina and whether they had had any problems when they were leaving the places in which they had resided before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell us how would the Muslim battalion react, or how did it react, when these things happened in Bijeljina where their families were living, or if such things happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: They would surely have complained and would not have continued to participate in the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony, Mr. Ljubojevic, and thank you for your devoted work in the interests of the people in Bijeljina and in Semberija.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR LJUBOJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, for everything you have done for the Serbian people in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Ljubojevic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank you all, and I wish you happy and successful work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are there any matters to be raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One at the behest of the Registry which is simply there was an issue about P6211 and whether the English transcript was the correct one, that was the transcript of ten pages, and Mr. Robinson and I confirmed to the Registry that it is the correct transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. There are some scheduling issues. Having just received the Mr. Karadzic Scheduling Order from the Appeals Chamber probably we need to vacate the sitting on the 17th of April. And one further issue is the -- in the week of 27th of May, the -- it is scheduled that the Chamber sit from Monday to Thursday, i.e., from 27th to 30th of May. I'm wondering whether it would cause any problem to the parties if the Chamber sits from Tuesday, i.e., 28th of May, to Friday, 31st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That will be no problem at our end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We have no reason to think so. But I suppose out of an abundance of caution, we can check the schedule -- the anticipated schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And, finally, yesterday the Chamber received a courtesy copy of a letter from Mr. Krstic which has been filed confidentially today. In this letter, Mr. Krstic reiterates that he refuses to testify in this case. Notwithstanding the position explained in his letter, the Chamber orders Mr. Krstic to appear before the Chamber at 9.00 a.m. on Monday, 25th of March, 2013, in line with the Chamber's oral ruling of 13th of March, 2013. The Registry is therefore instructed to advise Mr. Krstic and his counsel accordingly and to inform all relevant units in order to facilitate the transfer of Mr. Krstic to the Tribunal on Monday morning. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect, it occurs to me this may -- this type of specific information may be an additional factor that bears on the request the Prosecution made earlier with respect to such witnesses and that the Chamber ruled on this morning. The fact is now that Mr. Nicholls in particular will otherwise be here all weekend preparing extensively for cross-examination preparation for a witness who it appears will not be testifying. Under those circumstances, we would ask for some dispensation so that such a lavish expenditure of time does not take place and that we have some latitude with the beginning of cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I don't think I understood you in full. Could you expand your last sentence: "... some dispensation so that expenditure of time does not take place and that we have some latitude with the beginning of cross." Cross of who?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of Mr. Krstic in this case. What I'm indicating and what I have indicated before is, as the Court pointed out, the situation with such witnesses it that there is indeed a plethora of information. That means there is no end to the preparation which is required for such witnesses especially if there no indication what the witness will be testifying about and what the cross-examining counsel must focus on. And in cases where it appears that the witness will not testify at all, we have lawyers who are expending lavish time preparing for something that looks like won't happen. Now, in this instance, I'm trying to balance the efficiency of the courtroom with the efficiency of the expenditure of our resources. I would think that some level of preparation could be required so that Mr. Nicholls wouldn't be starting from scratch, but if he -- if he believes that he has to start immediately on the conclusion of direct examination no matter what subjects were covered, then he will be working around the clock to prepare for it. If there is some latitude given, and we understand that, if circumstances require, we can ask for a deferral which will be -- which we will receive, I think that's a much more fair approach to -- to take with respect to the use of our limited resources and our time at a point when -- when, really, many -- I think all the parties are working extremely hard and extremely long hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It sounds to me - I don't want to be very argumentative - but it sounds to me like this: Since there is a possibility that Mr. Krstic will not testify, you do not see the necessity or point of preparing at this moment. So if he, indeed, testifies, then the Prosecution would request for some deferral for the purpose of its preparation. Am I reading correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. With some clarifications on that. I understood the Court's ruling this morning and I'm not trying to ignore it by any means, that is, in its entirety. I'm trying to balance it in some way. So I'm not suggesting, for example, that based on what appears to be the realistic possibility that a particular witness won't testify, that nothing be done whatsoever. That would seem to be -- to fly directly in the face of the Court's ruling. I'm trying to accommodate the Court's concerns about time but in a fair way. On the other hand, I think in situation like this, given what appears to be the likelihood, it seems unfair to invest the amount of time that one would if that was a more realistic and -- and conventional probability. So I'm trying to balance that by noting that, of course, some preparation will take place, but if -- if it goes forward and involves issues that the Prosecution needs more time to address because -- because, for example, Mr. Nicholls wasn't here basically around the clock, that the Court would accept that the circumstances were such that that's a fair request, and -- and provide some latitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But would the position of the Defence be different from the Prosecution's? They should prepare as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, in this instance, Mr. President, we are prepared and will be ready to go forward with General Krstic. And we hope he changes his mind, and the reason is that we expect to ask him very few questions that can be very easily prepared. On the other hand, an attack on his credibility would understandably be more involved. If we were told that on Monday, you know, we were going to have no court and so you -- or else maybe there would be a 5 per cent chance that we would have court, wouldn't it be just human to say, okay, in the 5 per cent -- instead of working on this 5 per cent chance, let's just cancel it and we don't have to spend all of our time preparing for something that is very unlikely to occur. So that is what Mr. Tieger is basically saying. I don't understand why the Chamber has difficulty with that. It is just a normal request that ought to be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber made it clear that there may be instances where, good cause having been shown, a delay is warranted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: And given the expression by Mr. Krstic, which is very unequivocal at this point, this is a good example of good cause, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This may become all moot. But let me consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: In a spirit of what I suspect is a mixture of comprise and playing poker rather than playing chess, if I was Mr. Nicholls, I would not spent too much of my time this weekend engaging on cross-examination. And having heard that hint, if I were Mr. Nicholls, and things turned out differently, he could expect and should be able to expect a reasonably sympathetic hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May I just -- Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff reminded me, of course, that we wouldn't have enough information about the end of May to -- to assess the change in schedule against that. So we -- then we -- like Mr. Robinson, we have no objection to the Court's shift in the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The schedule will be changed accordingly. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of March, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
